I have mentioned that he was a poet. He published his first poem at twenty-three, and the entire nation greeted it with delight and enthusiasm. Fortune seemed always to favour him; no reputation had ever been established so swiftly, or spread so widely. The crowds praised the very poems that astonished the scholar in his study. Not a single dissenting voice was heard.

At this time, at the height of his fame, he met Elinor. She was an exquisitely beautiful young heiress living in the care of her guardian. From their first appearance together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor did not possess Woodville’s genius, but she was generous and noble. Her youth and the love she inspired wherever she went lifted her above any knowledge of what was not virtuous and excellent. She was lovely, with open, unaffected manners; her deep blue eyes glowed with a radiance that could come only from sensitivity joined with wisdom.

They were suited to one another, and soon fell in love. For the first time, Woodville experienced love’s happiness. Elinor was thrilled to hold the heart of someone so beautiful and so distinguished among his fellow men. Could anything but undiluted joy come from such a bond?

Woodville was a poet, welcomed eagerly in every social circle, and whenever he appeared every eye turned toward him alone. Yet he was a poor clergyman’s son, while Elinor was a wealthy heiress. Her guardian had no objection to their mutual affection: Woodville’s gifts were too exceptional to allow complaints about his smaller fortune. But her father’s final wishes forbade her to marry before coming of age, and her inheritance depended on her obedience. She had only just entered her twentieth year, so she and her lover had to accept the delay. Nevertheless, they were constantly together, and their happiness seemed like paradise. They studied together and planned their future pursuits. Drawing love and delight from one another’s looks and conversation, they hardly complained of the wait before their complete union. Woodville’s fame continued to grow, while the guidance of her accomplished lover made Elinor ever lovelier and wiser.

In two months Elinor would turn twenty-one, and everything was ready for their marriage. How can I tell of the catastrophe that ended so much happiness? Yet the earth would not be the blighted, sorrowful place it is if even one pair of such angelic beings had been allowed to live for each other. Search the whole world, and you will never find the perfect happiness their marriage would have brought them. The established order of life among us miserable inhabitants of the earth would have needed to be overturned to permit such absolute joy.

I got up early the next morning and once again managed to slip past my watchful creditors. Hurrying to the bookseller’s stall, I spent the small amount of cash I had on several books about mechanics and practical astronomy. Once safely home with them, I devoted every free moment to reading, and soon learned enough about these subjects, in my judgment, to carry out my plan. During breaks from my studies, I did everything possible to appease the three creditors who had made my life so difficult. Eventually I succeeded, partly by selling enough household furniture to pay half what I owed, and partly by promising to settle the remainder when I completed a small project I claimed to be planning. I also asked them to assist me with it. Since they were ignorant men, these measures made it fairly easy to enlist them in my scheme.

“With those arrangements made, I set about selling my remaining possessions with my wife’s help, exercising the greatest caution and secrecy. I also borrowed small sums under various pretexts, giving no thought to how I might repay them, until I had accumulated a substantial amount of cash. Using these funds, I bought materials at intervals: very fine cambric muslin in twelve-yard lengths; twine; a supply of rubber varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and various other items needed to construct and equip an exceptionally large balloon. I instructed my wife to sew the balloon as quickly as possible and explained precisely how she should proceed. Meanwhile, I fashioned the twine into a net of sufficient size, fitted it with a hoop and the required ropes, and purchased a quadrant, a compass, a telescope, an ordinary barometer with several important alterations, and two less familiar astronomical instruments. I then found opportunities to transport supplies by night to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam. These comprised five iron-banded casks holding roughly fifty gallons each and a sixth, larger cask; six suitably shaped tubes of tinned metal, each three inches across and ten feet long; a quantity of a particular metallic substance, or semi-metal, which I will not identify; and twelve demijohns of a very common acid. The gas produced from these last materials has never been generated by anyone other than myself—or at least has never been put to a comparable use. I would readily reveal the secret if it did not rightfully belong to a resident of Nantes, in France, who shared it with me under certain conditions.

I cannot express the ecstatic relief with which I turned from political quarrels in our own country and physical suffering in distant lands to my beloved home: that chosen dwelling of goodness and love, of peace and the exchange of every cherished feeling. Had I never left Windsor, I would not have felt these emotions so strongly. But in Greece I had been at the mercy of fear and terrible upheaval; there, after a time of anxiety and grief, I had watched two people pass away whose very names stood for greatness and virtue. Such suffering, however, could never enter the family circle that remained to me while we lived peacefully, secluded in our dear forest. The advancing years did bring certain small changes, and time, as always, left the mark of mortality upon our pleasures and hopes. Idris, so affectionate as a wife, sister, and friend, was a tender, devoted mother. Motherhood was no pastime for her, as it was for many; it was a passion. We had had three children, and the second had died while I was in Greece. That loss had mixed fear and sorrow with the triumphant joy of being a mother. Until then, these little creatures born of her, these young heirs to her fleeting life, had seemed assured of continued existence. Now she feared that the merciless destroyer would seize her surviving darlings as it had taken their brother. The slightest illness sent spasms of terror through her; any separation from them made her miserable. She had stored all her happiness in their fragile lives and remained constantly alert lest the stealthy thief steal these precious jewels as it had before. Fortunately, she had little actual cause for alarm. Alfred, now nine, was an honest, manly little boy, with a bright forehead, gentle eyes, and a temperament both kind and independent. Our youngest was still an infant, but his soft cheeks bloomed with health, and his tireless liveliness filled our home with innocent laughter.

Clara had outgrown the age whose speechless unawareness aroused Idris’s fears. Idris loved her, as everyone did. She combined such intelligence with innocence, such sensitivity with patience, and such seriousness with perfect good humour. Her extraordinary beauty and endearing simplicity made her a pearl among our most cherished possessions, a treasure of excellence and wonder.

At the beginning of winter, our nine-year-old Alfred began attending Eton. He saw this as his first step toward manhood and was correspondingly delighted. Studying and playing with others brought out the finest qualities in his character: his patient determination, his generosity, and his firmness tempered by self-control.
